The test separately exercises the actual set flux, null inputs, unequal raw transitions with equal weighted flux, one site, and the two-bit absorbing-state obstruction. No aggregate build or model submission was run.

The null split is valid. For two null atoms the weights vanish; if only x is null, evaluate the transition into x using the positive-start law at y. Each F_i(y) contains y, hence has positive mass, and every compatible numerator is mu({x})=0. The outgoing kernel at x need not vanish and is only multiplied by zero. Swapping x and y handles the other case.

With two supported starts, site compatibility is symmetric. At a compatible site the retained coordinates and thus the two fibers agree; the flux is the same product of atom masses over the common positive fiber mass. Incompatible site contributions both vanish. The Lean proof derives retained-tuple equality via funext and Fin.succAbove_ne, rewrites the same denominator, uses finite-sum distributivity and commutative multiplication, and retains the common weight. The countable-space bridge consumes this universal identity; the prose specializes the same rearrangement to finite sums over A and B.

Taking A=X gives invariance because K(y,X)=1. For the half-and-half 00/11 target at n=1, in either retained fiber through a supported state that state is the only supported point. Each such state is absorbing; starting at 00 leaves delta_00 at all times, which differs from mu on {00}. The actual-kernel test verifies reversibility, K(00,{00})=1 and mu({00}) != 1, not an explicit theorem about convergence of iterates.

The public-dev family random-scan-null-atoms is correct. The public sogb-006 asks for the null-atom subcase, why null mass is insufficient for arbitrary kernels, and an irreducibility counterexample. This item shares the null argument and diagonal example, but also requires the positive-positive compatible-site flux calculation and the atomic-to-set implication.
